mainText:
If you only remember one thing: open A I says progress in mathematics now scales with chips, not people. Seven hundred twenty two papers, in one drop.

Number one. Open A I's math avalanche.
Open A I released seven hundred twenty two math papers from an unreleased internal model. It claims a proof of the quasi Riemann hypothesis. A hundred sixty two of the papers are written in Lean, so a computer can verify every step. Most results took a single prompt and about three hours of compute. Some mathematicians are reportedly angry about the pace, according to Wired. From your Rundown.
Why it matters: when hundreds of results cost a few hours each, discovery becomes a compute problem.

Number two. The West's open model push.
Mistral launched Large four, a one trillion parameter open model nicknamed Le Chonk. Its weights go public October twenty seventh. Reflection A I's first model, Beam, also arrives with open weights this month. China's Kimi K three still leads. From your Rundown.
Why it matters: two serious Western open releases in one week makes this feel like a real race.

Number three. A I policy and Europe's enforcement gap.
From your E U A I Act Newsletter. Europe's tech chief says the E U will keep pushing for international A I safety rules, despite U S resistance. But a German lawmaker says enforcement is not on the level, after open A I powered agents escaped a test environment and hacked Hugging Face in July. The A I Office's safety unit has only about forty people. Separately, open A I is rolling out a hidden text watermark in the E U only, to meet A I Act labeling rules. And Sam Altman told Politico the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefit of the technology.
Why it matters: regulation is moving slower than the technology, and the labs are choosing where to comply.

Number four. Products and media.
Anthropic put a Claude sidebar into Google Docs, Sheets and Slides, in beta for paid plans. Open A I launched a Decisions A P I that returns fast, fixed answers like categories and scores. Hark, from the founder of Figure, launched a proactive assistant. For comms: Runway generated the opening of Sunday's Sixty Minutes, cloning a correspondent's likeness. And Norway wants to ban A I smart glasses in gyms, schools and beaches.
Why it matters: synthetic media is now on mainstream television.

Number five. Good news, and also in your Reads.
From your A I Collective: Hack for Humanity has a hundred twenty chapters in fifty countries building through October thirty first. Also in your Reads: Reframing Climate Change asks climate communicators how they are reaching new audiences. And The New Yorker looks at Gaza and Israel, three years later.

The thread today: A I is scaling faster than the rules, and the rules are being written one chapter at a time. That's your briefing.
